prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part for B044 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. Round 1 did not test the scientific case, because every member arrived at it independently, but it did sharpen what the case is. The discovery is a chain of three separable and necessary steps: Holst's human physiology of proglucagon-derived GLP-1 and its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action, Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the biologically active truncated peptide, and Drucker's biology of GLP-1 and GLP-2 and of receptor action. Together they converted a gut-hormone concept into a mechanism that could be targeted, and the field has changed accordingly. Maturity is not in question: independent laboratories confirmed the mechanism, and large randomized outcome trials show stable benefit in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The prize is for a discovery, and the discovery has three clear names within the cap. I have also asked myself whether the chair's questions should move me to a different structure, and they do not: a second part would have to be paid for from the same three-person budget, and no candidate outside B044 offers a trio that is both scientifically complete and fairly attributed.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weak point and round 1 did not resolve it. Mojsov's priority on the active GLP-1(7-36) form is publicly contested, Joel Habener's group is not among the credited names, and I cannot adjudicate the primary record from the supplied evidence. The cost of excluding Lotte Bjerre Knudsen is real. The half-life extension by acylation turned a peptide with a plasma half-life of minutes into a therapy, and the clinical impact we cite depends on it. I now hold that the exclusion must be defended only on two narrow grounds, the three-person cap and the discovery framing, and the citation must say so by wording and not by silence. A last risk is that a prize with this visibility is read as a prize for a commercial drug class and not for a biological mechanism.

responses.point: Leaving out Knudsen should be a deliberate choice because the Nobel Prize does not compensate omissions elsewhere, and a trio from B001 is harder to defend than the B044 trio; he places CAR-T above optogenetics.
responses.response: I agree that the Knudsen exclusion has to be deliberate, and I take your point that 'other recognition' is not a safe argument. In round 1 I called her work largely pharmaceutical, and I now think that wording was too dismissive. I would defend the exclusion only through the cap and the discovery framing, and I would keep the citation on physiology and the active peptide so that it reads as a statement about what is being honored and not as a verdict on her contribution. I also agree on B001: the channelrhodopsin discovery and the neuronal application are separable, and no trio does justice to both. That is a reason to wait, not a reason to compress the credit.

responses.point: She holds B012 as her first alternative because Mori and Walter are a clean pair, while accepting that impact is mainly conceptual; she also doubts that Rosenberg can be defended in a CAR-specific citation without Eshhar.
responses.response: We share the same two alternatives, B012 and B018, but I order them differently now. On the chair's question about a second part, I do not think B012 is excluded by weak science, since the Mori and Walter attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. It is excluded by the cap. Three names for B044 leave no seat for a second part, and two-person pairing would require dropping one of Drucker, Holst or Mojsov, which the attribution does not support. I accept your point that a two-part prize would also dilute the citation for the case with the strongest evidence of benefit. On B018 I agree that a trio including Rosenberg and not Eshhar is a judgment I cannot fully defend, so it stays an alternative and not a second part.

responses.point: As chair he asks whether the Mojsov credit can be kept at full weight given Habener's absence, and whether the committee wants a second part; he says the cap forces a narrow, explicit exclusion of Knudsen.
responses.response: On Mojsov, the supplied credit supports a distinct step, the identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide, and I would keep her at full weight. A public priority dispute is a reason to read the primary record carefully, not a reason to discount her. I would record openly that Habener's group worked in the same area, that he is not on the credited list, and that the committee can credit only the supplied names. That is a statement about the evidence we hold and not a ruling on the historical record. On a second part I answer no, for the reason above: the cap leaves no room, and B018 has an attribution gap (Eshhar, Rosenberg) that I would not accept as a second prize part.

responses.point: He prefers a single-achievement prize and resolves the discovery-versus-development concern by crediting the physiology and active peptide; he also keeps Sabatini in his TOR configuration on scientific grounds.
responses.response: I agree with the single-achievement structure and with resolving the concern by confining the credit to physiology and the active peptide, but I would no longer say that Knudsen's work is simply industrial and downstream. It is decisive for the therapy and we should say so in the record. On B013, where I disagreed with you in round 1, I will now concede part of the point: your argument that Sabatini's mTORC1 work is scientifically substantial and should be judged on the record, not on unverified allegations, is one I accept. I still regard Hall and Schreiber as the foundational pair and Sabatini's work as later, so B013 remains outside my alternatives, but I would reach that view on scientific sequence and not on conduct.

responses.point: He accepts the three-name B044 set but insists the half-life extension is what turned the peptide into a usable therapy, and wants the citation to credit translation to therapy so the omission is not read as a judgment on Knudsen.
responses.response: I agree with your premise and I have changed my emphasis because of it. The question is whether the citation should name therapy. My answer is to keep the phrase 'made incretin-based treatment possible', which acknowledges the translation to patients, but not to credit analogue design as part of the discovery, because that would imply a fourth name we cannot seat. Whether that wording is enough to prevent the omission from being read as a verdict on Knudsen is a legitimate doubt, and I do not claim to have settled it. I would rather accept that cost openly than widen the citation beyond what three laureates can support.

uncertainties: Whether the supplied three names capture the right allocation of credit for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, given Habener's group is outside the credited list and the public priority dispute with Mojsov.

Whether the citation wording 'made incretin-based treatment possible' sufficiently signals that the Knudsen exclusion reflects the cap and the discovery framing and not a judgment of her contribution.

Whether B012 should rank above B018 as the fallback beyond B044: B012 has a clean pair but limited clinical translation, while B018 has proven clinical effect but an unresolved Eshhar and Rosenberg attribution problem.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. My documented Salk co-authorship with Ronald Evans and my collaboration with Johan Ericson concern people not on any shortlisted ballot, and my co-authorship with Per Svenningsson (including the chair) and a single 2009 paper with Abdel El Manira do not bear on the GLP-1 case or on any alternative I list. I have no tie to any credited name on this shortlist and see no need for recusal.
